issues.legal_issue: A limited interest created for the first time by a will in the owner’s self-acquired property does not become absolute merely because it is granted to a Hindu woman, when the property itself is not given in lieu of maintenance.
material_facts: The testator made a will dividing his self-acquired property between his son and his second wife.
The wife received a restricted life interest, with the property to pass absolutely to the son after her death.
The wife was to receive income from the property for her livelihood; the property itself was not allotted in lieu of maintenance or to satisfy a pre-existing right.
The testator had also provided for the wife’s maintenance needs through the income and allowed her to mortgage property for a daughter’s marriage if necessary.
issues.conclusion: The wife’s interest remained a restricted life estate and did not enlarge into absolute ownership; the purchasers from her could not acquire a better title than she held.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 14(1) and 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 must be read so that Section 14(1) enlarges a limited interest where an instrument recognises or confirms a pre-existing right, including a right to maintenance, while Section 14(2) applies when an instrument creates a new and independent title subject to restrictions. Under V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy, a maintenance right is pre-existing, and a transfer that merely recognises it does not create a new title. But a property owner may devise self-acquired property by will subject to a limited estate if the property itself is not given in lieu of maintenance. The court distinguished Shakuntla Devi v. Kamla and Jupudy Pardha Sarathy v. Pentapati Rama Krishna, which concerned pre-1956 wills. The word “possessed” in Section 14(1) is wide and does not require physical possession, but the woman must have a vestige of a claim, right, or title.

rule.if: testamentary_property_dispute and owner_created_restricted_interest and property_itself_not_given_for_maintenance and maintenance_needs_provided and remainder_given_to_another_beneficiary

predicates.testamentary_property_dispute: The case concerns rights in property disposed of by a will.
predicates.owner_created_restricted_interest: The property owner’s instrument gave a woman a restricted interest rather than an absolute interest.
predicates.property_itself_not_given_for_maintenanc: The property was not transferred to the woman in satisfaction of a pre-existing right to maintenance.
predicates.maintenance_needs_provided: The owner made provision for the woman’s maintenance apart from giving her the property itself.
predicates.remainder_given_to_another_beneficiary: The instrument directed that the property pass to another beneficiary after the woman’s limited interest ended.
predicates.restricted_estate_remains_limited: The woman’s restricted interest does not become absolute merely because she received it under the instrument.

issues.definition: When a property disposition gives a woman a newly created restricted interest, does not give the property itself in lieu of maintenance, provides separately for her maintenance, and gives the remainder to another beneficiary, the restricted interest remains limited.

issues.legal_issue: A final adjudication of a transferor’s rights in property binds later claimants who derive their title from that transferor when the governing law has not changed.
material_facts: In earlier litigation between the son and the wife, the courts held that the wife had only a limited interest and could not alienate the property.
That adjudication was affirmed through the appellate process, and the challenge to it was dismissed by the Supreme Court.
The later purchasers claimed through the wife, whose rights had already been adjudicated.
The High Court treated the earlier adjudication as non-binding on the basis that the law had changed, but the Supreme Court found that the relevant law had not changed between the proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The earlier adjudication remained binding on the wife and on those deriving title from her; she could not create rights for later claimants contrary to that adjudication.
issues.legal_principle: The finality of an adjudication applies to later claims derived from a party whose rights were determined in the earlier litigation. The court rejected the High Court’s reliance on Shakuntla Devi v. Kamla and Mathura Prasad Bajoo v. Dossibai N.B. Jeejebhoy because there had been no intervening change in the law. The prior judgment binding the transferor could not be avoided by conveying property to third parties.

rule.if: later_title_dispute and prior_final_adjudication_of_same_title and transferor_bound_by_prior_adjudication and claimant_derives_title_from_transferor and no_change_in_governing_law

predicates.later_title_dispute: The case involves a later dispute over rights in property previously litigated.
predicates.prior_final_adjudication_of_same_title: A final judgment in earlier litigation determined the relevant property rights.
predicates.transferor_bound_by_prior_adjudication: The person who later transferred the property was bound by the earlier judgment.
predicates.claimant_derives_title_from_transferor: The later claimant asserts rights obtained from the person bound by the earlier judgment.
predicates.no_change_in_governing_law: The legal rule governing the property rights did not change between the earlier and later proceedings.
predicates.prior_adjudication_binds_successors: The earlier judgment binds later claimants whose asserted rights derive from the party bound by it.

issues.definition: When a final judgment determined the same property rights, binds the transferor, and the later claimant derives title from that transferor without an intervening change in governing law, the judgment binds the later claimant.

issues.legal_issue: Purchasers who acquire property through transactions made in the course of, or following, repeated unsuccessful challenges to the transferor’s title are not bona fide purchasers entitled to defeat the rights established by the prior adjudication.
material_facts: The transferor’s daughter had obtained a collusive decree concerning the property and then granted a lease, but the decree and lease were set aside.
The transferor’s limited interest was upheld against her through the appellate process, including before the Supreme Court.
The transferor nevertheless executed sale deeds for portions of the property during the continuing litigation.
The purchasers claimed protection as bona fide purchasers under Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.
issues.conclusion: The purchasers were not bona fide purchasers; their transactions were dubious and did not defeat the rights established in the earlier litigation. They could not obtain a better title than the transferor had.
issues.legal_principle: Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 was invoked as protection for bona fide purchasers, but the court found the purchasers’ transactions not bona fide in light of the history of collusive and unsuccessful attempts to defeat the established rights, and the transfers made during the litigation. A transferee cannot obtain a better title than the transferor possessed.

rule.if: property_purchase_dispute and transferor_title_repeatedly_challenged_unsuccessfully and transfer_made_during_or_after_litigation and purchaser_claims_through_transferor

predicates.property_purchase_dispute: The case concerns a purchaser’s claim to rights in property acquired from another person.
predicates.transferor_title_repeatedly_challenged_u: The transferor or persons acting for the transferor made repeated unsuccessful attempts to assert rights inconsistent with the established title.
predicates.transfer_made_during_or_after_litigation: The transfer to the purchaser occurred while litigation over the property was ongoing or after the transferor’s claim had been rejected.
predicates.purchaser_claims_through_transferor: The purchaser relies on title derived from the person whose rights were challenged.
predicates.purchaser_is_not_bona_fide_and_cannot_de: The purchaser is not treated as bona fide and cannot use the purchase to defeat the title established by the litigation.

issues.definition: When a purchaser derives title from a transferor whose claim has repeatedly failed and acquires the property during or after litigation over that title, the purchaser cannot be treated as bona fide or defeat the established title.

issues.legal_issue: A second appeal under the applicable regional courts law does not require framing a substantial question of law when the Code of Civil Procedure provision imposing that requirement does not apply.
material_facts: The High Court decided a second appeal brought under the Punjab Courts Act, 1918.
The High Court did not frame a substantial question of law.
The Supreme Court treated the procedural point as settled by its Constitution Bench decision in Pankajakshi v. Chandrika.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not required to frame a substantial question of law in deciding the second appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Under Pankajakshi v. Chandrika, Section 97(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 does not apply to a second appeal under the Punjab Courts Act, 1918, and therefore the requirement to frame a substantial question of law does not govern that appeal.

predicates.second_appeal_under_regional_courts_law: The proceeding is a second appeal brought under a regional courts law.
predicates.civil_procedure_question_requirement_ina: The procedural requirement to frame a substantial question of law under the general civil procedure code does not apply to that proceeding.
predicates.substantial_question_of_law_not_required: The court may decide the second appeal without framing a substantial question of law.

issues.definition: When a second appeal is governed by a regional courts law and the general civil procedure requirement to frame a substantial question of law does not apply, that question need not be framed.
